newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan reaffirms west-to-east mining rights shift.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan reaffirms west-to-east mining rights shift.

text.p: The economics ministry on Tuesday reaffirmed its commitment to end all mine exploration rights in western Taiwan in 1997, a move aimed at promoting cement-making in the island's relatively underdeveloped east.

The ministry said its Industrial Development Bureau had recommended ending all mining rights in western Taiwan to help promote the cement industry's development in eastern Taiwan, a policy promoted by minister Wang Chih-kang.
"This is the ministry's final decision," a spokeswoman told Reuters. "It follows Minister Wang's recent comments that we will keep our promise to end western mining rights"
The policy needs final approval from the cabinet, which was expected to agree, officials said.
The announcement was expected to end a bitter stalemate in Taiwan Cement's plans to build a T$80 billion cement project in the eastern county of Hualien.

Taiwan Cement, one of the island's two top cementmakers, threatened in May to halt the Hualien investment if Taiwan's government reversed its pledge to promote eastern development by ending mine exploration rights in western Taiwan.
The ministry has vowed to end all cement makers' mine exploration rights in western Taiwan by the end of 1997 and had urged local makers to move their operations to eastern Taiwan.
The strategy, aimed to boost eastern Taiwan's lagging economy, had sparked complaints from environmentalists.
Eastern Taiwan's higher production costs have made most makers hesitant to move. Only Taiwan Cement followed the policy and in so doing was left at a competitive disadvantage.
Taiwan Cement has said it had heard the ministry planned to extend mining rights in western Taiwan, a move it denounced as unfair.
Taiwan Cement's Hualien plan, which includes a cement plant, power plant and industrial harbour in the government-designated Hoping cement zone, has been dogged by political problems.
In December 1995, the firm said it was suspending the T$80 billion investment project because of serious environmental protection protests there.
Since the environmental protests eased in late 1996, the company has gradually re-launched the project.
Taiwan Cement has said it already had invested T$2 billion in preparatory works on the project.
